title: The Sun of Wisdom Dispels Transgressions
author: Zhanran (annotated)
excerpt: Deluded thoughts are the cause of all karma; if one is not driven by deluded thoughts, there is no cause for creating karma. If one can cut off a deluded thought with a single thought at its very arising, the accumulated roots of past karma are eliminated on the spot.

inline.s: (The Dream Wanderings Collection,
“Instruction to Dong Zhiguang.”)

Deluded thoughts are the cause of all karma; if one is not driven by deluded thoughts, there is no cause for creating karma. If one can cut off a deluded thought with a single thought at its very arising, then the accumulated roots of past karma are eliminated on the spot.

[The scholar Dong Sizhang, born and raised in a house of wealth and honor, early gave rise to the mind seeking to transcend birth and death — this was the power of his past cultivation of the excellent conditions of prajñā, which had been perfuming him from within. He first called upon Master Yunqi, who transmitted to him the Pure Land teaching. Soon after, he came to pay his respects to this old man at Shuangjing, wishing to receive the upāsaka precepts. He also confessed of his own accord that his karmic offenses were deep and grave, and begged for the essential means of escaping suffering — by what practice could his transgressions be extinguished? The old man thereupon instructed him, saying:]

Dong Sizhang, born and raised in a wealthy and noble family, early resolved to end birth and death — this was the power of his past-life cultivation of the excellent conditions of prajñā perfuming him from within. He first called upon Master Lianchi, who transmitted to him the Pure Land teaching. Soon after, he came to pay respects to me at Shuangjing, wishing to receive the upāsaka precepts. He also confessed that his karmic offenses were deep and grave, and begged for the essential means of escaping suffering: by what practice could his transgressions be extinguished? Thereupon I instructed him, saying:

[The upāsaka precepts] “Upāsaka” means a male lay follower. The upāsaka precepts are the five precepts: not to kill, not to steal, not to commit sexual misconduct, not to lie, and not to drink intoxicants.

[The student already knows that the roots of his offenses are deep and grave. The worthy ones of old taught people: “At all times dissolve past karma, and by no means create new calamities.” For sentient beings whose karma is heavy, the Buddha opened the single gate of repentance, which is the foremost expedient for escaping suffering. A verse says: “The host of transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them. If you wish to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true appearance.” This is the principal practice; apart from it, everything else is a supporting expedient.]

The worthy ones of old taught: “At all times dissolve past karma, and by no means create new calamities.” The gate of repentance that the Buddha opened for sentient beings whose karma is heavy is the foremost expedient for escaping suffering. A verse says: “The host of transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them. If you wish to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true appearance” (later the text says, “the mind that is free of things — this is the true appearance”). This is the principal practice; apart from it, everything else is a supporting practice.

[The host of transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them] Just as the sun melts frost and dew, so contemplating the true appearance (the sun of wisdom) can dispel the host of transgressions. The Sūtra of Contemplating the Bodhisattva Universal Virtue's Dharma Practice says:

“The vast ocean of all karmic hindrances arises entirely from deluded thoughts. If you wish to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true appearance. The host of transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them.”
[The ocean of karmic hindrances] Karmic hindrances as deep and vast as the great ocean. [Sit upright and contemplate the true appearance] Later the text says:
“The mind that is free of things — this is the true appearance.”

[The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddhas; it is originally undefiled and has no mark of birth and death, coming or going. It is only because of the initial non-awakening — being deluded about one's original self-nature — that it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, all manner of deluded thoughts arise, with every kind of inversion, creating every kind of karma and deludedly grasping the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance: not comprehending one's own mind, one is turned by deluded thoughts. It is like a person in deep sleep having one bad dream after another — all manner of scenes, all manner of terror, with suffering hard to bear. When he wakes and seeks the things of the dream, they cannot be found at all. So it is that sentient beings, fallen into the dream of ignorance, follow deluded thoughts in inversion, create every kind of karma, and bring suffering upon themselves. Viewed with waking eyes, how can these inverted states possibly exist?]

The self-nature of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddhas; it is originally without defilement, and without any mark of birth and death, coming or going. But because of the initial non-awakening — being deluded about one's original self-nature (entering the dream of ignorance) — this is ignorance. Because of ignorance, all deluded thoughts arise, and thus every kind of inversion occurs, creating every kind of karma and deludedly grasping the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance: not comprehending one's own mind, one is turned and dragged along by deluded thoughts. It is like a person in deep sleep having one bad dream after another — all manner of scenes, all manner of terror, with suffering hard to bear. When he wakes and seeks the things of the dream, they cannot be found at all. Sentient beings are likewise: fallen into the dream of ignorance, they follow deluded thoughts in inversion, create every kind of karma, and bring suffering upon themselves. Viewed with waking eyes, how can these inverted states still exist?

[Since we are now presently in the dream of ignorance, how can past karma be dissolved? One must use the light of wisdom to illuminate and shatter ignorance, and truly believe that one's own mind is originally pure; if one is not driven by deluded thoughts and inversions, then all karma is without a cause, for deluded thoughts are the cause of all karma. Why is this so? Because, from beginningless time, being deluded about one's own mind, one has, life after life, created all manner of karma with the deluded mind. These karmic habits have accumulated within the field of the eighth consciousness, irrigated by the water of ignorance, causing these evil seeds to put forth the sprouts of karma. This is the root of offenses, from which all evil karma arises.]

Then, being now presently in the dream of ignorance, how can one dissolve past karma? One must use the light of wisdom to illuminate and shatter ignorance, and firmly believe that one's own mind is originally pure; if one is not driven by deluded thoughts and inversions, then there is no cause for creating karma, for deluded thoughts are the cause of all karma. Why is this so? Because, from beginningless kalpas, being deluded about one's own mind, one has, life after life, created all manner of karma with the deluded mind. These karmic habits have accumulated in the ālaya consciousness (the eighth consciousness), irrigated by the water of ignorance, causing these evil seeds to put forth the sprouts of karma. This is the root of offenses, from which all evil karma arises.

[Now, to dissolve past karma, one must first bring forth the great light of wisdom to illuminate and shatter ignorance, not permitting deluded thoughts to sprout and secretly grow. If one can cut off a deluded thought with a single thought at its very arising, then the accumulated roots of past karma are eliminated on the spot. This is what is meant by “do not fear the arising of thoughts; only fear that awareness comes late.” If the light of awareness is a little late, one is turned by it. If, in the arising of thought in daily activity, one is aware of each thought and dissolves each thought, this is what is meant by “the host of transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them.” Because the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is called “wisdom can dispel them.”]

Now, to dissolve past karma, one must first bring forth the great light of wisdom to illuminate and shatter ignorance, not permitting deluded thoughts to sprout and secretly grow. If one can cut off a deluded thought with a single thought at its very arising (a single sudden flash of awareness), then the accumulated roots of past karma are eliminated on the spot. This is what is meant by ‘do not fear the arising of thoughts; only fear that awareness comes late.’ If the light of awareness is a little late, one is turned by it (the deluded thought). If, in the arising of thought in daily activity, one is aware of each thought and dissolves each thought, this is what is meant by “the host of transgressions are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dispel them.” Because the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom, this is how wisdom can dispel the host of transgressions.

[If, without ceasing by day or night, you diligently and constantly observe, never letting a thought pass unchecked, but directly, at the place where deluded thoughts arise, investigate to the utmost that there is no mark of arising — looking and looking, in the end nothing can be grasped — then after a long time of ripening, your own mind is pure and free of things. The mind that is free of things is the true appearance. If you constantly contemplate this mind, what deluded thought can find room, what accumulated karma can find a lodging? Applying the mind in this way is called the samādhi of contemplative illumination.]

You must, without ceasing by day or night, diligently observe, never letting a thought pass unchecked, but directly, at the place where deluded thoughts arise, investigate to the utmost that there is no mark of arising. Looking and looking, the deluded thought can in the end be grasped not at all. After a long time of ripening, your own mind is pure and free of things. The mind that is free of things is the true appearance. If you constantly contemplate this pure mind, what deluded thought can find room, and what accumulated karma can find a lodging? Applying the mind in this way is called the samādhi of contemplative illumination.

[If, without ceasing by day or night, you diligently observe] Here the word “ruo” means “you” (thou). For example: “If I change your duty and restore your taxes, how would that be?” (This line, from Liu Zongyuan's The Snake-catcher's Tale, means: “If I replace your duty of catching poisonous snakes and restore your taxes, what do you think?”)

[If one's own mind has coarse and heavy afflictions, so that one is not aware of the places where ignorance obstructs — in such a case, the worthy ones of old had a method of teaching people to investigate: take the verified kōan of reciting the Buddha's name and apply one's strength right there. Raise up the sound of the Buddha's name and set it across your chest, and then investigate: after all, who is the one reciting the Buddha? Thus, raise it and investigate it together, never letting it go empty. Set this ball of doubt across your chest like your very life-root, never letting it go. Amid all movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, coming and going, sitting and standing, there is only this one matter and no other. Applying the mind in this way, the moment you see a deluded thought arise, press it with this huatou, and it is shattered on the spot; all deluded thoughts are naturally wiped out without a trace. For this huatou is like the sun at high noon, illuminating every hidden place. One only fears that one's mental effort may slacken and that one may be unwilling to keep it truly stirred, and therefore be unable to withstand the deluded thoughts. If one can withstand them, then where the deluded thoughts dissolve is precisely the time when past karma is dissolved. Setting aside this one move and seeking outside the mind, even if all the Buddhas appeared in the world, there would be no place of repentance. This lies in one's own power; it cannot be substituted by the power of another.]

If one's own mind has coarse and heavy afflictions, so that one is not aware of the places where ignorance obstructs (when deluded thoughts arise). If this is the case, the worthy ones of old had a teaching for people to investigate: take the verified kōan of reciting the Buddha's name (“who is reciting the Buddha?”) to cut off deluded thoughts. The method is: raise up the sound of the Buddha's name and set it across your chest, and then investigate — after all, who is the one reciting the Buddha? Thus, raise it and investigate it together, never letting it go empty. Set this ball of doubt across your chest like your very life-root, never letting it go. Amid all movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, coming and going, sitting and standing, there is only this one matter and no other. Applying the mind in this way, the moment you see a deluded thought arise, press it with this huatou, and the deluded thought is shattered on the spot. Investigating in this way, all deluded thoughts are naturally wiped out without a trace. For this huatou is like the sun at high noon, illuminating every hidden place. One only fears that one's own mental effort may slacken and that one may be unwilling to keep it truly stirred, and therefore be unable to withstand the deluded thoughts. If one can withstand them, then where the deluded thoughts dissolve is precisely the time when past karma is dissolved. Setting aside this one move and seeking outside the mind, even if all the Buddhas appeared in the world, there would be no place of repentance. This matter requires one's own effort entirely; it cannot be substituted by the power of another.

[To stir up (tisi)] To be vigilant and alert, maintaining right mindfulness. It also refers to the work of concentrating on investigation amid walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. The Gateless Barrier of the Chan Tradition says: “With all three hundred and sixty joints and eighty-four thousand pores of your whole body, raise up a single ball of doubt and investigate the word ‘wu’ (no), keeping watch by day and night.” The Complete Works of Master Zhu,

in the chapter “Nourishing the Mind,” says: “Only keep constant watch over yourself, accumulate it bit by bit, and after a long time it will naturally continue on and merge into one seamless whole.” For example, Master Ruiyan asked himself every day: “Master, are you awake?” and answered himself: “Awake.” [Awake] Clear-minded and alert.

[If one's evil habits are strong and overpowering, so that one's strength cannot withstand them — in the past the Buddha had a clear instruction: if a practitioner's habitual tendencies cannot be removed, he should single-mindedly recite the mind-mantra spoken by my unconditioned mind-Buddha. This is truly an extraordinary expedient. Because each person's store-consciousness has an undercurrent, and the habitual tendencies are deep and thick, one's wisdom-power cannot reach them. Where one cannot reach, one must rely on the Buddha's mind-seal to break them secretly. It is like a robber who is hard to defeat: one must request the sword of the imperial workshop. This must be done at the two periods of morning and evening, arranging the time according to one's own convenience; but the work of investigation remains the truth of the first principle.]

If one's evil habits are strong and overpowering, so that investigation cannot withstand the deluded thoughts, then in the past the Buddha had a clear instruction: “If a practitioner's habitual tendencies are hard to uproot, he should single-mindedly recite the mind-mantra spoken by my unconditioned mind-Buddha.” This is truly an extraordinary expedient. Because each person's store-consciousness has an undercurrent, and the habitual tendencies are deep and thick, one's wisdom-power cannot reach them. Where one cannot reach, one must rely on the Buddha's mind-seal to break them secretly. It is like a robber who is hard to defeat: one must request the sword of the imperial workshop. This must be done at the two periods of morning and evening, arranging the time according to one's own circumstances and reciting as a fixed practice. In short, the work of investigation must remain the principal practice.

[Mind-mantra] A general term for dhāraṇī. A dhāraṇī is the most excellent dharma within the Tathāgata's mind, hence it is called the “mind-mantra.” Fascicle Seven of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra says: “The unconditioned mind-Buddha radiates light from the crown of the head and, seated upon a jeweled lotus, speaks the mind-mantra.” [The sword of the imperial workshop] A sword specially made by the imperial workshop for the emperor's own use. In ancient times, when the Son of Heaven dispatched a minister to handle a major case, he would often bestow the sword of the imperial workshop, signifying the grant of full authority to execute first and report afterward.

[With this instruction, the old man was very much like giving a blind man a walking stick; the actual carrying out lies in one's own person, and cannot be done by one's teachers or friends on one's behalf. Because the layman aspired to return to the Dharma gate, he was given the name Fujue (“blessed awakening”), meaning that he should take luminous awareness as the root of his practice. He was given the courtesy name Zhiguang (“wisdom light”), for if not by the light of wisdom, how else could the darkness of ignorance be broken? One need only keep one's luminous awareness undimmed, and when the light of wisdom appears before one, that is precisely the time for ending karmic hindrances and transcending birth and death.]

This instruction of mine is very much like giving a blind man a walking stick; the actual carrying out lies entirely in oneself, and cannot be substituted by one's teachers or friends. Because you have resolved to practice, I give you the name Fujue (“blessed awakening”), meaning that you should take luminous awareness as the root of practice. I give you the courtesy name Zhiguang (“wisdom light”), for if not by the light of wisdom, how else could the darkness of ignorance be broken? You need only keep your luminous awareness undimmed, and when the light of wisdom appears before you, that is precisely the time for ending karmic hindrances and transcending birth and death.

[One's own person] To do it personally. [Courtesy name (zi)] The courtesy name, a person's alternate name, expressing the meaning of the given name or one's character and virtue. For example: surnamed Liu, given name Bei, courtesy name Xuande. In usage, when referring to oneself one uses the given name to show humility; when addressing another one uses the courtesy name to show respect.
